Learning Objectives
Understand the etiology and clinical evaluation of limb-length discrepancy.
Recognize the goals of preoperative radiographic templating in total hip arthroplasty.
Recognize methods for intraoperative clinical assessment of limb length and offset.
Appreciate surgical methods for restoring accurate limb length and offset.
Anatomy and Biomechanics

The goals of total hip arthroplasty are achieving appropriate limb length and femoral
offset to restore appropriate hip biomechanics. Equalization of functional limb length
allows for improved gait. Restoration of appropriate offset improves hip biomechanics
via proper tensioning of the abductor muscle complex and contributes to stability and
wear properties of the prosthesis.
Limb-Length Discrepancy
Actual limb length is the distance between the anterior superior iliac spine and the medial
malleolus. Functional discrepancy is based on patient perception.
Functional limb-length discrepancy may be secondary to a suprapelvic obliquity, such as a stiff
spine; intrinsic pelvic obliquity, such as acetabular wear; or infrapelvic obliquity, such as
femoral pathology.
Limb-length inequality after total hip arthroplasty may be associated with numerous
postoperative clinical complications, including nerve palsies, back pain, and abnormal gait.

Limb-Length Discrepancy
Actual and functional limb-length discrepancy should be evaluated. Actual limb length is
measured radiographically as the distance between the anterior superior iliac spine and
the medial malleolus. Functional limb-length discrepancy is based on patient perception
and is determined by placing blocks of a known height beneath a standing patient’s
affected limb until the patient feels the limbs are equal in length. Functional
discrepancies may result from soft-tissue contractures or fixed lumbosacral and pelvic
obliquity.
If the actual and functional limb lengths differ, determining the source of the
discrepancy is important. This can be accomplished by evaluating pelvic obliquity.
Compare the height of the hemipelves in standing and sitting positions. Suprapelvic
obliquity originates from spinal pathology; in this situation, pelvic obliquity will not
change between standing and sitting positions. Intrinsic pelvic obliquity originates from
pelvic bone or cartilage loss, whereas infrapelvic obliquity originates from femoral or

tibial pathology. Intrinsic and infrapelvic obliquity will resolve with sitting1 (Resource 1;
Figure 1).
Figure 1 Illustrations show hip contractures. A, A hip adduction contracture causes a
patient to perceive the involved leg as shortened. B, A hip abduction contracture causes
a patient to perceive the involved leg as lengthened. If a patient has a flexible spine,
these false limb-length differences should not be corrected with the use of implants.
Postoperatively, the contracture will resolve, the spine will adjust, and limb lengths will
be equal. (Reproduced from Engh CA Sr: Optimizing stability and limb length, in
Lieberman JR, Berry DJ, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Hip. Rosemont, IL, American

Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2005, pp 167-176.)
Limb-length inequality after total hip arthroplasty may be associated with numerous
postoperative clinical complications, including nerve palsies, back pain, and abnormal
gait. In addition, patient dissatisfaction with leg-length discrepancy after total hip
arthroplasty is a substantial cause of litigation against orthopaedic surgeons.
Although rare, reported peroneal nerve palsies occur after a mean of 2.7 cm of
lengthening, whereas sciatic nerve palsies occur after a mean of 4.4 cm of lengthening;
however, neurologic insults occur with as little as 1.3 cm of lengthening2 (Resource 2).
Although no established safe threshold exists, progressive lengthening is associated with
increased risk of nerve injury. Shortening of the limb may lead to abductor dysfunction
and instability and low back pain. Surgeons must discuss the risk of limb-length
inequality with patients preoperatively. Patients should understand that intraoperative
matching of limb lengths may not be possible, especially if lengthening is necessary to
achieve stability.
Nonsurgical management of limb-length discrepancy includes a trial of observation and
physical therapy. If these treatment modalities fail, shoe lifts can be prescribed;
however, this is not always tolerated by patients. In general, the authors of this lesson
recommend waiting at least 3 months postoperatively before offering a shoe lift. In
patients with persistent pain and dysfunction or neurologic injury, revision arthroplasty
is an option.2
Offset Discrepancy
Femoral offset is the distance between the long axis of the femur and the femoral head center
of rotation.
Restoration of appropriate femoral offset is important for implant stability.
Increased offset decreases joint reaction forces, whereas decreased offset increases joint
reaction forces.
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
4/16


Offset Discrepancy
Femoral offset is the perpendicular distance between a line bisecting the long axis of the
femur and the femoral head center of rotation (Figure 2). Offset contributes to the
stability of the prosthesis by decreasing bony impingement and tensioning the abductor
muscle complex. It also affects the joint reaction force within the hip. Increased offset
decreases the joint reaction force by increasing the moment arm for the abductor
muscles to balance the counteracting body weight. Conversely, decreased offset leads to
higher joint reactive forces and has been shown to contribute to increased polyethylene
wear; however, this may be less relevant with highly cross-linked polyethylene3
(Resource 3). Failure to restore offset may lead to abductor weakness, a Trendelenburg
gait, and dislocation secondary to inadequate muscle tension. Tall or large male patients
may have a higher native offset than that possible to be re-created; these patients
should be counseled accordingly with regard to the risk of dislocation. Excessive offset
beyond that necessary for stability should be avoided because it may lead to
trochanteric bursitis.
Preoperative Planning
Templating
Preoperative templating for total hip arthroplasty should be performed using an AP
radiograph of the pelvis, with the hips in 15° of internal rotation and a 25-mm marker ball to
correct for magnification.

Templating
Preoperative templating is performed before total hip arthroplasty to create a surgical
plan for component size and position that accurately reconstructs limb length and offset.
Templating is performed using an AP radiograph of the pelvis centered over the pubic
symphysis. A marker ball of known size, typically 25 mm, can be used to correct for
radiographic magnification. The hips are internally rotated 10° to 15° to match femoral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Limb Length and Offset
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
5/16

neck anteversion and create a true AP view. External rotation of the hips, implied
radiographically by increased visualization of the lesser trochanter, may result in
underestimation of true femoral offset. Limb-length discrepancy is determined by
measuring side-to-side differences between fixed points on the pelvis and the femur.
Surgeons can template off the diseased hip or the contralateral hip.
Radiographic Landmarks
Limb-length and offset discrepancies can be measured radiographically using fixed points on
the pelvis and femur.

Radiographic Landmarks
Pelvic and femoral landmarks are used to establish preoperative limb-length and offset
discrepancies. To evaluate limb lengths, a horizontal reference line is drawn through
reproducible pelvic landmarks, such as the acetabular teardrops or the most distal
aspect of the ischial tuberosities. The vertical distance is measured between this
horizontal line and a fixed point on the femur, such as the tip of the greater trochanter
or the proximal corner of the lesser trochanter and compared side to side (Figure 2).
Figure 2 AP pelvic radiographs demonstrate femoral offset, leg-length difference,
femoral head diameter, and endosteal diameter determined via digital templating. A,
The femoral offset of the right hip is 48 mm, the femoral head diameter is 46 mm, the
right hip is 4 mm longer than the left hip, and the endosteal diameter is 14.5 mm. B, The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
6/16

femoral offset of the left hip is 29.5 mm, the femoral head diameter is 42.5 mm, the left
hip is 3 mm shorter than the right hip, and the endosteal diameter is 15 mm.
(Reproduced from Garvin KL, Hartman CW: Preoperative planning and templating in total
hip arthroplasty, in Lieberman JR, Berry DJ, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Hip, ed 2.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 73-78.)
Femoral offset discrepancy can be evaluated by comparing differences in the
perpendicular distances between a line bisecting the long axis of the femur and the
center of rotation of the femoral head. Ensuring proper rotation of the femur is
important for a true AP view of the femoral neck because external rotation will result in
underestimation of the offset.
Acetabular Templating
The acetabular cup should be templated in 40° of abduction at the native center of rotation.
The lateral edge of the acetabular component should sit at the lateral rim of the acetabulum,
and the cup should not be medialized beyond the ilioischial line.

Acetabular Templating
Begin templating by placing the acetabular component at the lateral edge of the
teardrop. The cup should be placed in 40° of abduction compared with a horizontal
reference line through both teardrops. The lateral aspect of the acetabular component
should sit on the lateral rim of the acetabulum; however, this may vary depending on
patient anatomy. Cup medialization was previously advocated to decrease joint reactive
forces and reduce wear rate by shortening the body weight moment arm; however, as
the wear properties of implants have improved, this has been surpassed by the goal of
preserving bone stock, and a more lateral cup position is acceptable, especially if
necessary to optimize offset. The goal is to maximize surface area contact and
component coverage without medializing the cup beyond the medial wall of the
acetabulum. The center of rotation of the acetabular component template should be
placed anatomically at the native acetabular center of rotation. The templated cup
center of rotation is used as a reference point for reconstruction of length and offset.

Surgeons should note the relationship of the templated cup to the surrounding bony
landmarks, including the superolateral acetabular rim and the medial edge of the
teardrop, which represents the base of the cotyloid fossa4,5 (Resources 4 and 5; Figure
3).
Figure 3 Weight-bearing AP pelvic radiograph with the lower extremities in 10° to 15° of
internal rotation demonstrates a stepwise approach for templating total hip
arthroplasty. 1, The digital image is calibrated with markers. 2, Pelvic axis orientation is
determined using a line (long orange line) across the teardrops. 3, Leg lengths are
determined using the distance from a line perpendicular to the pelvic axis (short orange
lines) and the tops of the lesser or greater trochanters. 4, The acetabular component
(blue outline) is placed to restore the hip center of rotation, with the cup apex just lateral
to the teardrop at 40° to 45° of abduction from the pelvic axis. 5, The femoral
component (blue outline) is templated to determine the best fitting stem and stem sizes
to restore femoral lateral offset and equalize leg lengths. (Reproduced from Pulido LF,
Incavo SJ: Imaging of the hip and knee for primary and revision arthroplasty, in Mont MA,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
8/16

Tanzer M, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Hip and Knee Reconstruction, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 3-14.)
Femoral Templating
The femoral component template should adequately fill the canal without overlying the
endosteal cortex.
The difference in location between the templated center of rotation of the femoral head and
the center of rotation of the acetabular component represents the change in length and offset.

Femoral Templating
The femoral component should be sized to fit within the cortices of the femoral canal,
and press fit stems should adequately fill the canal. If the implant overlies the endosteal
cortex at any point, the component is oversized and will not fit. Femur fracture may
occur if the larger templated stem size is inserted. The templated femoral head center of
rotation should be marked on the implant template, and its position can be adjusted by
altering component size, neck length, or offset, depending on the available options. The
difference in location between the templated center of rotation of the femoral head and
the center of rotation of the acetabular component represents the change in length and
offset. If the templated femoral head center of rotation lies proximal to the acetabular
center of rotation, the leg will be lengthened. If it lies medial to the acetabular center of
rotation, the offset will be increased. After the appropriate size and position of the
femoral stem is selected, the planned neck cut height is measured from the proximal
edge of the lesser trochanter to the base of the templated neck of the stem.4
Intraoperative Assessment
Limb Length
On the surgical table, limb-length discrepancy can be grossly estimated at the knee during
total hip arthroplasty with the patient in the lateral decubitus position or at the heels/medial
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Limb Length and Offset
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
9/16

malleoli during total hip arthroplasty with the patient in the supine position.
Intraoperatively, the surgical effect on limb length can be measured as the change in distance
between fixed points on the acetabulum and femur. The position of the capsular flap also can
be used.
During total hip arthroplasty with the patient in the supine position on an orthopaedic surgical
table, fluoroscopy may be used to assess limb lengths by comparing preoperative and
intraoperative ipsilateral radiographs or by comparing the surgical side with the contralateral
side.

Limb Length
Radiographic limb-length discrepancy should be established preoperatively based on
templating. Intraoperatively, the discrepancy also should be evaluated on the surgical
table to allow for assessment of any changes that occur with implantation of the
prosthesis. This can be accomplished in several ways.
After lateral positioning and draping, the difference in femoral lengths can be measured
at the knee with the use of a ruler. Awareness of the position of the pelvis is important
because pelvic tilt will affect the relative positions of the legs. In general, the surgical leg
will appear short because it is slightly adducted (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration of a lower extremity shows intraoperative comparison of limb
lengths with the patient in the lateral decubitus position. The relative position of the
femurs is recorded. (Reproduced with permission from Engh CA Jr: Optimizing stability
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Limb Length and Offset
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
10/16

and limb length, in Lieberman JR, Berry DJ, eds: Advanced Reconstruction Hip, ed 2.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 167-176.)
After surgical exposure, additional methods can be used. To establish fixed points on the
pelvis and femur, a Steinmann pin can be placed in the pelvis proximal to the
acetabulum, and a location on the greater trochanter can be marked with the use of a
tag stitch. The change in distance between these points measured before femoral head
osteotomy and again with trial implants in place represents the change in leg length.
Calipers also can be used to measure vertical and horizontal distances between fixed
points on the pelvis and femur to help assess length and offset changes6 (Resource 6).
Alternatively, a flap of the posterior hip capsule can be tagged immediately after
capsulotomy. This tag stitch is lifted directly anteriorly so the suture overlies the greater
trochanter. The greater trochanter is marked along the length of the suture via
electrocautery to mark its position. After trial implants are in place, the new location of
the capsular tag stitch is assessed in reference to the electrocautery mark to measure
change in limb length. If the new location of the tag stitch is proximal to the
electrocautery mark, the limb has been lengthened. In addition, the distance from the
lesser trochanter to the center of the femoral head can be measured intraoperatively
and compared with preoperative templating measurements. The accuracy of this
intraoperative measurement depends on placing the acetabular component in the same
position as that on the template.
Finally, an intraoperative radiograph can be obtained with the trial implants in place to
directly evaluate limb length. Although often helpful, this radiograph may be deceiving.
Obtaining a high-quality AP pelvis radiograph is difficult if the patient is in the lateral
decubitus position on the surgical table. Close attention to the position of the coccyx
relative to the pubic symphysis and the relative size of the obturator foramen are
important to ensure rotational accuracy.
During total hip arthroplasty with the patient in the supine position on a standard
surgical table with the limbs draped free, limb-length discrepancy can be measured
grossly at the heels or the medial malleoli. Ensuring that pelvic obliquity is perpendicular
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Limb Length and Offset
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
11/16

to the long axis of the surgical table is important for this method. Fluoroscopy also may
be used. Fluoroscopy is necessary if the patient is in the supine position on an
orthopaedic surgical table with the feet immobilized in traction. A preoperative AP image
of the hip can be compared with an image in the same projection with the trial or final
implants in place. Alternatively, if the fluoroscopy machine can capture the entire pelvis
in one image, the surgical extremity length may be compared with the contralateral
extremity. Length measurement methods similar to those already described, such as the
distance between the acetabular teardrop and a point on the lesser trochanter, should
be used. Relative offset changes can be measured using the distance between the lesser
trochanter and a vertical line through the center of the pubic symphysis; however, this
requires the legs to be positioned similarly in both images. Changes in
adduction/abduction or flexion/extension will falsely alter the measurements.
Offset
Intraoperatively, offset can be measured using a caliper, the capsular flap, or an intraoperative
radiograph.

Offset
The preoperative template should aim to re-create native offset. If the preoperative plan
is followed, then reasonable approximation of offset can be expected; however,
appropriate offset must be confirmed intraoperatively. Similar to limb length, a caliper
may be used for offset. Offset is measured as the change in horizontal distance between
fixed points on the pelvis and femur. A capsular flap also can be used to estimate offset.
This is accomplished by lifting the capsular flap superiorly and noting the position of the
flap edge in relation to the posterior edge of the greater trochanter. Increased distance
between the edge of the capsular flap and the trochanter with trial implants in place
indicates increased offset. The abductor muscle tension can be used as an approximate
estimation of offset, with increasing tension representing increasing offset; however,
muscle tension also will be affected by limb-length changes. Finally, an intraoperative
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:34 PM
AAOS | Limb Length and Offset
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002064
12/16

radiograph can be obtained with trial components in place to evaluate offset7 (Resource
7).
Reconstruction
Reconstructing appropriate limb length and offset can be accomplished by varying femoral
stem size or position, using modular head and neck length options, or altering acetabular cup
position.

Reconstruction
Limb length and offset can be altered intraoperatively by adjusting the location or size of
the components. Limb length can be increased by upsizing the femoral component,
causing the implant to sit higher than the level of the neck cut. Length can be decreased
by downsizing and sinking the stem further down the canal below the level of the neck
cut. Varying modular head and neck length options are available; however, increasing
neck length often leads to increases in offset and overall length. Independent of the
head and neck length, stems often come with an increased offset stem option. Complete
understanding the implant system being used is important for determine the changes
that will occur with each implant option. Most femoral stem systems have a standard
and a high offset option that does not affect leg length. During preoperative templating,
the optimal offset option should be selected and confirmed with the trial broaches
during the procedure.
Placement of the acetabular cup directly also affects length and offset. The cup should
be placed according to the template by using landmarks, such as the base of the cotyloid
fossa and the superolateral acetabular rim. Placing the cup higher in the pelvis will cause
elevation of the center of rotation and shortening of the limb, whereas placing the cup
inferiorly will cause lengthening. Although femoral offset is independent of the amount
of cup medialization, increasing cup medialization will decrease abductor tension and
may lead to instability. Offset may need to be increased through the stem to account for
overmedialization of the cup. Similarly, leaving the cup excessively lateral may over-

13/16

tension the abductors and may require a reduced femoral offset option to achieve
appropriate muscle tension.
